analysis.one_liner: Adds outpatient prescription drug coverage to Medicare, with government-set payment limits and no formularies.
analysis.headline: The Medicare prescription drug bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and died without ever getting a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made Medicare Part B pay for prescription drugs filled at the pharmacy — a benefit Medicare did not offer in 2001. After a $250 yearly deductible, Medicare would pay 80% of the cost, up to a government-calculated payment limit for each drug. It barred the government from excluding any drug or drug class from coverage (no formulary), barred pharmacies from charging seniors more than the general public, required pharmacies to counsel patients about drug interactions, and set price surveys of wholesalers with fines for false answers.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries — seniors and people with disabilities — who in 2001 had no drug coverage under Medicare and paid pharmacy bills out of pocket or through private supplemental plans. They would gain coverage for essentially all FDA-approved prescription drugs, a cap on what pharmacies could charge them, a physician guide to cheaper drug alternatives, and mandatory counseling about drug interactions and cheaper equivalent drugs.

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Part B would pay for covered outpatient prescription drugs and biologicals, a benefit Medicare did not provide in 2001.
Medicare would pay 80% of the lesser of the actual charge or a set payment limit, after a $250 deductible in 2003 (waived for first-year immunosuppressive drugs after an organ transplant).
The Secretary would be barred from excluding any covered outpatient drug, drug class, or FDA-approved use from coverage — no formulary.
Participating pharmacies could not charge Medicare beneficiaries more than they charge the general public, and violations could draw civil money penalties.
Participating pharmacies would have to offer counseling on proper drug use and potential drug interactions, and advise beneficiaries when a therapeutically equivalent drug is available.
The Secretary would survey wholesale drug prices, could fine wholesalers up to $10,000 for refusing to answer or giving false answers, and payment limits would be set on a national basis.

Physicians would receive an annual guide comparing average wholesale prices of at least 500 of the most commonly prescribed drugs, grouped by condition, to steer prescribing toward lower-cost options.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers and the Medicare Part B trust fund, which would finance the new drug benefit; the review commission would be paid from the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund. Pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear reduced effective prices through payment limits and price surveys, and private Medicare insurance plans would lose much of their drug-coverage business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, drug makers, private Medicare plans

drawbacks.text: Beneficiaries face a $250 deductible in 2003 (rising with Part B premium inflation) and then 20% coinsurance with no annual out-of-pocket cap, so a beneficiary on expensive drugs would have unlimited cost exposure.
No prescription could cover more than a 30-day supply (longer only up to 90 days in limited cases), meaning more trips to the pharmacy and more dispensing events.

Payment limits are built on 'average wholesale price,' a published list price that historically ran well above the prices pharmacies actually paid, risking overpayment to the industry unless surveys corrected it.
The bill pays for the new benefit out of the Medicare Part B trust fund without an identified funding source, a cost an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

As drafted, the Prescription Drug Payment Review Commission would be appointed by the 'Director of the Congressional Office of Technology Assessment' — an office Congress had abolished in 1995 — a drafting error that would have had to be fixed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: drug coverage for the roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries who in 2001 mostly paid for prescriptions out of pocket. The design has real weaknesses — no cap on the 20% coinsurance leaves the sickest seniors exposed, and the AWP-based payment limits could overpay manufacturers. On balance it is a broad benefit for older and disabled Americans financed by taxpayers, with price limits that would have pressed drug makers on costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, then sent to Health subcommittees, and never got a markup or a vote before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. Eliot Engel introduced the bill on January 31, 2001, with five original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction, with jurisdiction to be determined later by the Speaker.
Both committees referred the bill to their Health subcommittees (February 15 and March 14, 2001), and the bill never advanced further.
It attracted 8 cosponsors, all Democrats, and received no action in the second session of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers came out ahead: a Medicare drug benefit with payment limits, mandatory price surveys, and an explicit no-formulary rule never advanced, so no government price pressure or guaranteed beneficiary volume was imposed. Private Medicare plans also kept their drug-coverage business untouched. Congress did not enact any Medicare drug benefit during this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug makers and private Medicare plans

sides.party_line_note: All 9 supporters in the record — the sponsor and 8 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.note: The bill would set payment limits per drug, survey wholesale prices with fines for false answers, and bar the Secretary from excluding any drug from coverage — a government purchaser paying set prices for every FDA-approved use. A benefit covering all seniors' prescriptions in exchange for price limits was the trade the bill offered; its death left manufacturers' pricing untouched.

Pharmacies would become the mandatory dispensing channel for the new benefit, with a $5 dispensing allowance ($3 for non-participating) and prompt monthly payment, in exchange for accepting assignment and never charging Medicare beneficiaries more than the general public. The bill would lock in their role as the dispensing gateway while regulating what they could charge seniors.

Direct Medicare drug coverage would crowd out the supplemental drug coverage private plans sold to seniors, and the bill imposed accounting and deductible-coordination rules on plans that reimbursed drugs. Their interest was in keeping drug coverage a private product; beneficiaries' interest was in getting it from Medicare directly.
